title: Ninety Seconds of Fun

pages.text:
Saturday fifteen felt flat, like eating a cracker that has lost its salt.

Gus roared at 6:47, and I let him. By 7:22, the smoke alarm was screaming, and Dad was standing on his chair, fanning the air with a dish towel while his face lit up with anticipation.

"Max! Good morning! Did you know I'm reading a book about anti-gravity?"

I opened my mouth to say no, which was the correct answer. But my mouth didn't wait for permission. It just said, "It's impossible to put down!"

Dad blinked. He looked at me, then at the toaster, then at me again. His mustache twitched.

"Did you just...?" he started.

"No," I said, though my voice sounded like it came from someone else. "I didn't."

But I had. I knew the punchline before he did. I knew every pun he would make that day. I knew the hot dish was tuna. I knew Jonah's text would say I HAVE A PLAN.

It was like knowing the ending of a movie. It doesn't make the movie better. It just makes it quieter. I watched Dad drop the towel. He looked confused. And for the first time, I noticed that a family isn't just people. It's surprise. And I had stolen all of it.
pages.image: Dad, a big man with a dark mustache and fish apron, stands on a chair looking confused; Max, an 11-year-old boy in a red hoodie, stands in the doorway with a blank expression; smoke fills the air.

pages.text:
Saturday nineteen, I wanted to do something big. Something that felt real, not just a loop.

Grandma Bea had just set her laundry basket down in the hall. She was humming, completely unaware that I was standing behind her, eyeing her purse. The keys to her green Buick hung on the strap, just metal teeth on a ring.

I took them. My hand shook, but I held them out, feeling the cold metal bite into my palm. I could drive to the edge of town, to the highest point, and just stop. Or go. It didn't matter. It was the act. The risk.

But then I looked at the clock on the wall. It was 12:01. In forty-nine minutes, I would be back in my bed, waking up to Gus roaring.

I put the keys back in the purse. My fingers were slippery, and I had to wipe them on my hoodie before I walked away.

I learned something important that Saturday. The loop made everything safe, but it also made everything meaningless. If I crashed the Buick, Grandma Bea would wake up with no memory of it. But I would remember the shake in my hand. I would remember the choice.

Even if nobody is watching, you are watching yourself. And I didn't like what I saw. I went to the kitchen and sat on the floor, hugging my knees, feeling very small and very awake.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy in a red hoodie, kneels on the kitchen floor hugging his knees; a set of car keys hangs from a purse on the counter nearby; the room is lit by soft afternoon light.

pages.text:
Saturday twenty-three. Jonah arrived at 2:00, helmet on, grinning wide enough to crack it.

He pulled the laminated itinerary out of his backpack. He didn't ask if I believed him. He just started talking. "First we go to the creek. Then we play minigolf. Then we eat ice cream. It is perfect. It is the best day of my life. And yours."

I watched his face. His eyes were bright, and he was so sure, so happy to be the one who knew the secret. It was beautiful. It was also a script. I knew exactly what he was going to say next. I knew he was going to ask, "So, do you believe me, Max?"

"I believe you," I said.

He beamed. It was the seventh time. I felt a lump in my throat that had nothing to do with sadness. It was just... full. I reached out and put my hand on his shoulder.

"I love you, man," I said.

Jonah froze. His grin vanished. He took a step back. His hand went to his helmet strap.

"Did you just say...?" he started.

"Yeah."

He looked around the garage, as if checking for witnesses. Then he reached into his pocket, pulled out a granola bar, and handed it to me.

"Eat this," he said, his voice high and shaky. "You look like you need sugar."

I started to laugh. It started as a snort, then a cough, then a howl. I laughed until my ribs hurt, until I couldn't breathe, until the sound stopped and I was just standing there, crying for no reason I could name.
pages.image: Jonah, an 11-year-old boy with a buzz cut and bike helmet, holds out a granola bar with a worried expression; Max, in a red hoodie, leans forward, laughing hard with tears in his eyes; a laminated paper is on the table between them.

pages.text:
Saturday twenty-eight. 3:00 PM.

I sat on the garage roof with a bag of pretzels, looking down at Larkspur Lane, where the sun felt warm on my neck and the wind carried the smell of cut grass from Mr. Grady’s yard. I knew every crack in the pavement, which mailboxes were painted green, and the exact shade of the sky, yet it was also the loneliest place I had ever been.

I was a boy in the middle of a town where nobody was surprised by him. I ate a pretzel, which was salty, and then I ate another, which was exactly the same.

There is a thing nobody tells you about a perfect anything. It is empty, like a video game level with no enemies to fight and no score to chase. I was the only person in my own life, and I was tired of being the only one. I looked at the street, then at the sky, then at my hands, wishing I could be wrong or new, but I was just Max Bello, repeating, again and again, to a world that had forgotten how to listen.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy with messy dark hair, sits alone on the edge of a garage roof holding a bag of pretzels; he looks out over a quiet residential street in late afternoon light.

pages.text:
11:58.

The house was quiet, the boxes were packed, and the clock ticked on the wall. I stood in the hall, looking at Gerald, while the little wooden bird stayed perfectly still. I didn't wish. I didn't say, "I wish today would never end." I didn't say anything at all. I just looked at the bird, feeling the day settle into my bones.

"How do I make this stop?" I asked.

Gerald did not move. He did not cuckoo. He just sat there with his crooked beak and angry eyebrows, watching me. I flopped onto the hall floor and stared up at the ceiling. I thought about the pancakes, then the Buick keys, and finally Jonah's granola bar. Maybe fun isn't the point. Maybe the day just has to be perfect, and then it lets me go.

I pulled my notebook from my pocket and found a clean page. I uncapped my pencil. I wrote, in big, bold letters: OPERATION PERFECT SATURDAY.

This is the part where things get worse.
pages.image: Max, an 11-year-old boy in a red hoodie, lies on his back on the wooden floor of a hallway, looking up at a cuckoo clock on the wall; he holds a notebook and pencil in his hand; the room is dimly lit by a small lamp.
